\subsection*{Related work}
\paragraph{Adaptive updates and convergence.}
Coordinatewise adaptation includes AdaGrad \cite{duchi2011adagrad} and
ADADELTA \cite{zeiler2012adadelta}. Adam combines averages of gradients and
squared gradients \cite{kingma2015adam}; AdamW applies weight decay separately
from this rescaling \cite{loshchilov2019adamw}. Earlier analyses separate
the roles of sign, magnitude and variance in Adam
\cite{balles2018dissecting}, and study updates that retain only gradient
signs \cite{bernstein2018signsgd}. Our question concerns the dependence
between the gradient and its rescaling, including their shared history.
Convergence guarantees for adaptive methods already cover several
nonconvex settings \cite{zaheer2018adaptive,chen2019adamtype}, sufficient
conditions on the averaging parameters \cite{zou2019sufficient}, and
proofs for Adam without changing its update rule
\cite{defossez2022simple,zhang2022adam}. These guarantees have specific
assumptions on parameters, steps or sampling; they do not imply convergence
for every fixed-memory constant-step problem studied here. Other methods
change the statistic in the denominator: AdaBelief uses gradient prediction
errors \cite{zhuang2020adabelief}. Our exact formula concerns AdamW's
squared-gradient denominator and is not a theorem for all adaptive methods.

\paragraph{The closest comparisons.}
The averaged Adam update as a function of the whole sampling distribution
has already been studied \cite{dj2024}; its derivative and noise covariance
also appear in Gaussian limit theorems for averaged Adam iterates
\cite{dj2026}. The effect of symmetric versus asymmetric noise is established
for quadratics with a fixed Hessian proportional to the identity
\cite{symmetry}. Adam's failure on stochastic convex problems is classical
\cite{reddi}. Recent deterministic AdamW analysis already gives unstable
equilibria and exact fixed-step stability conditions \cite{su}.
Large-step stability thresholds are studied for gradient descent
\cite{cohen_edge} and adaptive methods \cite{adaptive_edge}, with recent
Adam theory proving oscillation and gradient reversal \cite{eos}.
Our contribution is the smooth pair with all the matching
conditions above, the change from vanishing to persistent stationary error,
and an explicit condition that restores vanishing error. The denominator
offset and weight decay stay positive and fixed throughout.
Normalization-dependent floors versus SGD under multiplicative noise
also precede this work \cite{singh}. Here the optimizer remains the same
AdamW update with a fixed positive denominator offset, and only the pairing
changes while both full separate distributions remain fixed.

manuscript_citation_contexts:
\paragraph{Classical methods and stationary distributions.}
The study of noisy iterative root finding begins with stochastic
approximation \cite{robbinsmonro1951}. Its connections to differential
equations and stability are developed in
\cite{kushneryin2003,benaim1999,borkarmeyn2000}. Avoidance of unstable
points is also classical \cite{pemantle1990}; the decreasing-step conclusion
there is distinct from the stationary lower bound needed here.
Constant-step invariant distributions and small-step limits have established
theories \cite{fortpages,ddb,chenmoumaguluri2022}. Exact stationary balance
relations for SGD are studied in \cite{yaida2019}; such relations presuppose
stationarity and do not by themselves bound the time to reach it.
Corrections that turn dependent noise into a martingale are standard tools
in limit theorems with Markovian noise \cite{fort2015}.
Averaging iterates changes their limiting fluctuations
\cite{polyakjuditsky1992,mouetal2020}; our leading error concerns an
unaveraged stationary iterate. We use these established methods rather than
claiming that Gaussian limits, covariance equations or unstable-point
avoidance are themselves new.

\paragraph{Diffusion models and memory scaling.}
Stochastic differential equations provide approximations to optimization
over finite time intervals \cite{litaie2017}. Such models also describe
adaptive updates and their scaling rules \cite{malladi,compagnoni}.
Their Adam limits use memory parameters approaching one with the learning
rate; the main theorem here instead fixes both memory parameters.
An approximation over a fixed time interval does not automatically justify
interchanging the long-time and small-step limits. We retain AdamW's actual
random gradient history and prove statements for its stationary laws.
Our separate long-memory result takes the small-step limit first, so it
does not cover every simultaneous scaling of step and memory.
The counterexample applies to descriptions retaining only the matched
quantities. It does not rule out diffusion models that retain additional
dependence information.

\paragraph{Connections to transformers and limits of the example.}
Heavy-tailed gradient noise has been measured in neural networks
\cite{simsekli} and used to explain difficulties of SGD in attention models
\cite{zhang_attention}. Differences between Hessian blocks provide another
explanation for Adam's advantage on transformers \cite{zhang_hessian}.

\cite{kunstner2023noise}, and optimization speed need not predict held-out
performance \cite{wilson2017marginal}. Our bounded-noise quadratic examples
hold the whole Hessian distribution fixed and isolate an additional
dependence. They neither explain the full transformer optimization gap
nor establish a generalization or language-quality benefit.

manuscript_citation_contexts:
\paragraph{Connections to transformers and limits of the example.}
Heavy-tailed gradient noise has been measured in neural networks
\cite{simsekli} and used to explain difficulties of SGD in attention models
\cite{zhang_attention}. Differences between Hessian blocks provide another
explanation for Adam's advantage on transformers \cite{zhang_hessian}.
However, an SGD--Adam gap can remain even with full-batch gradients
\cite{kunstner2023noise}, and optimization speed need not predict held-out
performance \cite{wilson2017marginal}. Our bounded-noise quadratic examples
hold the whole Hessian distribution fixed and isolate an additional
dependence. They neither explain the full transformer optimization gap
nor establish a generalization or language-quality benefit.

manuscript_citation_contexts:
\paragraph{Optimizing the pairing.}
Extremal expectations under fixed separate distributions have classical
rearrangement bounds \cite{cambanissimonsstout1976}. We apply these bounds
to the exact AdamW response weight. The contribution is the resulting sharp
range of leading stationary errors and its connection to the optimizer,
rather than a new general rearrangement inequality.

The theorem gives the full range of possible leading errors in one
dimension. Pairing large curvature with small noise gives the lowest error;
pairing large curvature with large noise gives the highest. The step that
bounds an average product from its separate distributions is classical
\cite{cambanissimonsstout1976}. The AdamW-specific part is \eqref{eq:rowkernel} and
its decreasing weight. Appendices~\ref{app:kernel}--\ref{app:transfer}
prove that the averaged update points inward and that the actual stationary
error has the stated limit. Section~\ref{sec:phases} proves exact equality
of SGD errors for the matrix examples as well.
